courses.title: Community-Based Rehabilitation and Professional Practice
courses.description: Disability and rehabilitation in Nigeria, community-based rehabilitation, assistive technology, occupational and women's health physiotherapy, and physiotherapy ethics, law and practice management.

topics.title: Disability and Rehabilitation in Nigeria
topics.summary: Models of disability, prevalence, the Disability Act 2018 and rights-based approaches.

material.heading: Models and burden
material.body: Disability results from the interaction between people with impairments and attitudinal and environmental barriers (UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities — CRPD, 2006). Models: medical model (disability as an individual problem to be cured), social model (disability created by society's barriers — inaccessible buildings, transport, attitudes), and the biopsychosocial ICF model integrating both. WHO estimates about 15–16% of the world's population has a disability; in Nigeria, estimates suggest over 25 million people with disabilities, arising from stroke, trauma (road crashes, conflict), cerebral palsy, polio sequelae, leprosy, blindness, amputation (diabetes, trauma, bone-setter gangrene), and ageing. People with disabilities face poverty, exclusion from education and employment, stigma (including beliefs about curses) and poor access to health and rehabilitation services, which are concentrated in cities.

material.heading: Law and policy
material.body: The Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018 prohibits discrimination, requires accessibility of public buildings and transport (with a five-year transition period), provides for education, health care, employment (at least 5% of public sector jobs reserved for persons with disabilities) and established the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities (NCPWD). Nigeria ratified the CRPD in 2007. Rehabilitation (WHO: a set of interventions designed to optimise functioning and reduce disability in individuals with health conditions in interaction with their environment) is a core health service within universal health coverage — WHO's 'Rehabilitation 2030' call for action. Barriers in Nigeria: few rehabilitation professionals (physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech therapists, prosthetists and orthotists), out-of-pocket costs, poor referral and limited community services.

topics.title: Community-Based Rehabilitation
topics.summary: CBR principles, the CBR matrix, community workers and inclusive development.

material.heading: CBR principles
material.body: Community-based rehabilitation (CBR — now community-based inclusive development, CBID) is a strategy within general community development for rehabilitation, equalisation of opportunities, poverty reduction and social inclusion of people with disabilities, implemented through the combined efforts of people with disabilities, their families, communities, and health, education, vocational and social services (WHO, ILO, UNESCO). The CBR matrix has five components: health (promotion, prevention, medical care, rehabilitation, assistive devices), education (early childhood, primary, secondary, non-formal, lifelong learning), livelihood (skills development, self-employment, wage employment, financial services, social protection), social (personal assistance, relationships, culture and arts, recreation and sports, justice) and empowerment (advocacy, community mobilisation, political participation, self-help groups, disabled people's organisations — DPOs). Principles: participation, inclusion, empowerment, self-advocacy, accessibility, sustainability and equal opportunity.
keyPoints: Five components: health, education, livelihood, social, empowerment

material.heading: Implementation
material.body: CBR in Nigeria and Africa relies on community rehabilitation workers or volunteers trained to identify people with disabilities, provide basic therapy and home programmes, teach families, make simple assistive devices from local materials (e.g. walking frames, standing frames, adapted seats), refer to specialist services, and link people to schools and livelihood programmes. Physiotherapists act as trainers, supervisors, consultants and advocates. Home visits allow assessment of the environment and practical adaptations (ramps, grab rails, accessible toilets). Examples: rehabilitation of people after stroke at home, children with cerebral palsy (parent groups), leprosy self-care groups, and post-polio support. Challenges: sustainability and funding, volunteer retention, integration with government services, and measuring outcomes. Telerehabilitation (phone and video follow-up) extends reach, especially since COVID-19.

topics.title: Assistive Technology, Prosthetics and Orthotics
topics.summary: Mobility aids, wheelchairs, prostheses and orthoses, and amputee rehabilitation.

material.heading: Mobility aids and wheelchairs
material.body: Assistive technology maintains or improves functioning and independence; WHO estimates only about 1 in 10 people who need assistive products have access in low-income settings. Walking aids: walking sticks (held in the hand opposite the affected leg; handle at the level of the wrist crease/greater trochanter), crutches (axillary — top 2–3 finger-breadths below the axilla, weight through the hands; elbow crutches), and frames (for maximum stability). Gait patterns with crutches: non-weight-bearing (three-point), partial weight-bearing, four-point and two-point, swing-to and swing-through. Stairs: 'up with the good, down with the bad' (the crutches move with the affected leg going down). Wheelchairs must be appropriately sized and prescribed (WHO Wheelchair Service Training Package — assessment, prescription, fitting, user training, follow-up), with pressure-relieving cushions for users with spinal cord injury. Rough terrain wheelchairs suit rural Nigerian environments. Other assistive products: hearing aids, spectacles, communication aids and adapted utensils.
keyPoints: Up with the good, down with the bad

material.heading: Prosthetics, orthotics and amputees
material.body: Amputations in Nigeria commonly result from diabetic foot disease, trauma (road crashes, gunshot, explosions), gangrene after traditional bone setting, peripheral arterial disease and tumours. Amputee rehabilitation: pre-operative counselling, postoperative care — stump (residual limb) shaping with elastic bandaging (figure-of-eight, tighter distally) or shrinker socks, prevention of contractures (below-knee — avoid knee flexion; above-knee — avoid hip flexion and abduction; lie prone), strengthening, mobility training, phantom limb sensation and pain management (mirror therapy, desensitisation, medication), and early walking aids (pneumatic post-amputation mobility aids). Prosthetic fitting: socket (patellar tendon bearing for transtibial), pylon, foot (e.g. SACH foot); prosthetic gait training. Orthoses: ankle–foot orthoses (foot drop, spasticity), knee–ankle–foot orthoses (polio sequelae), spinal braces, splints for burns and hand injuries. Cost and limited prosthetic services (few prosthetists and orthotists — e.g. National Orthopaedic Hospitals) are major barriers; low-cost technologies (e.g. polypropylene, ICRC technology) help.
keyPoints: Causes: diabetes, trauma, bone setter gangrene

topics.title: Occupational and Women's Health Physiotherapy
topics.summary: Ergonomics and work-related disorders, antenatal and postnatal care, pelvic floor and continence.

material.heading: Occupational health
material.body: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are common among Nigerian workers: farmers (low back pain from bending and carrying), traders and head-load carriers (neck pain), artisans, drivers, office workers (neck and shoulder pain from computer use), and health workers (nurses and physiotherapists — back injuries from patient handling). Ergonomics fits the task to the worker: workstation adjustment (screen at eye level, feet flat, elbows at 90°, lumbar support), manual handling principles (assess the load, keep it close to the body, bend knees not the back, avoid twisting, use aids and team lifting), job rotation, rest breaks and exercise programmes. Physiotherapists perform workplace assessments, pre-employment screening, injury prevention education, rehabilitation and return-to-work programmes (graded work). Workers' compensation in Nigeria is covered by the Employee's Compensation Act 2010.

material.heading: Women's health
material.body: Pregnancy: common complaints include pelvic girdle pain, low back pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and diastasis recti; safe antenatal exercise (at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week for uncomplicated pregnancies — walking, swimming; avoid supine exercise after about 16 weeks, contact sports and overheating), pelvic floor muscle training, and antenatal classes (breathing and relaxation, positions for labour). Contraindications include ruptured membranes, pre-eclampsia, placenta praevia after 26 weeks, and cervical insufficiency. Postnatal: pelvic floor training, diastasis recti assessment and exercises, posture and lifting advice, return to exercise, and management of perineal pain. Urinary incontinence (stress — pelvic floor muscle training is first-line, supervised for at least 3 months; urge — bladder training), pelvic organ prolapse (pelvic floor training, lifestyle advice), and rehabilitation after obstetric fistula repair (pelvic floor exercises) and after breast cancer surgery (shoulder range, lymphoedema management — manual lymphatic drainage, compression, exercise, skin care).

topics.title: Professional Practice, Ethics and Management in Physiotherapy
topics.summary: MRTB regulation, ethics and consent, documentation, evidence-based practice and private practice.

material.heading: Regulation and ethics
material.body: The Medical Rehabilitation Therapists (Registration) Board of Nigeria (MRTB), established by Decree 38 of 1988, registers and regulates physiotherapists, occupational therapists, speech therapists, audiologists and prosthetists/orthotists; it approves training programmes, conducts professional examinations, issues annual practising licences and disciplines misconduct. The Nigeria Society of Physiotherapy (NSP) is the professional association (member of World Physiotherapy). Physiotherapy education in Nigeria has moved to the Doctor of Physiotherapy (DPT) degree in many universities. Nigerian physiotherapists practise as first-contact (autonomous) practitioners in many settings. Ethical principles: autonomy (informed consent for assessment and treatment, including manual therapy and intimate examinations — chaperones), beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, confidentiality, and professional boundaries. Misconduct includes practising without a licence, sexual misconduct, false claims, and treating beyond competence. Continuing professional development is required for licence renewal.

material.heading: Documentation, EBP and management
material.body: Documentation follows SOAP (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) or problem-oriented medical records, with outcome measures recorded to show progress; notes must be accurate, timely, legible and signed — they are legal documents. Evidence-based practice combines research evidence (databases such as PEDro — Physiotherapy Evidence Database with PEDro scale ratings of RCT quality), clinical expertise and patient values; clinical practice guidelines guide care (e.g. low back pain — education and exercise over passive modalities). Electrophysical agents (ultrasound, TENS, interferential, shortwave diathermy) should be used selectively with evidence, observing contraindications (e.g. over malignancy, pregnant uterus, pacemakers for some agents, impaired sensation). Service management: planning, budgeting, staffing, quality improvement (audit), outcome measurement, marketing and patient satisfaction. Private practice requires business planning, registration of premises, record-keeping, pricing and insurance; health insurance coverage of physiotherapy is limited in Nigeria. Interprofessional collaboration and referral pathways improve patient outcomes.
